title: Non-Right-Angled Trigonometry

findings.finding: Explain how enlargement changes the common sine-rule ratio.
findings.breakdown: Distinguishes equal ratios within one triangle from a numerical constant shared by all triangles.
findings.checked: The sine rule is established in nr-p6-formula and nr-p11-proof. Similarity supplies unchanged corresponding angles. Multiplying every side by three multiplies each ratio by three.
findings.assumptions: Similar triangles are prior knowledge from the separately taught Similar Triangles booklet.

repair.proposal: Optional task after nr-p11-conclusion: Triangle ABC has a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = k. A similar triangle has every side three times as long. Find its three side-to-sine ratios without calculating angles. Is k the same for every triangle? Explain. Expected answer: all three ratios become 3k because corresponding angles remain unchanged. The common value need not be the same across triangles.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain both equality within a triangle and the effect of enlargement on the common value.

findings.finding: Vary the included angle while holding two side lengths fixed.
findings.breakdown: Exposes how the opposite side changes and connects the cosine rule with Pythagoras’ theorem at 90 degrees.
findings.checked: nr-p19-formula and nr-p21-example supply the method. The proposed answers are correct: sqrt(52), 10, sqrt(148), and approximately 6.09. All included angles define valid triangles. The supplied practice has no equivalent fixed-side run.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator in degree mode is available.

repair.proposal: After nr-p22-q2: Before calculating, predict the order of the opposite side lengths. Two sides are 6 cm and 8 cm. Find their opposite side to 2 d.p. when the included angle is (a) 60 degrees, (b) 90 degrees, (c) 120 degrees. Explain what happens as the included angle increases. Expected answers: 7.21 cm, 10.00 cm, 12.17 cm; the opposite side increases. Only the included angle varies. Follow with an unpatterned question: two sides are 5 cm and 9 cm with included angle 40 degrees; find the opposite side to 2 d.p. Expected answer: 6.09 cm.

findings.doneWhen: Students predict, calculate and explain the side-length relationship, then apply the method to the unpatterned question.

findings.finding: Explain how the included angle controls area for fixed side lengths.
findings.breakdown: Connects maximum area and equal areas for supplementary angles to the established area formula.
findings.checked: nr-p32-rule and nr-p37-proof establish A = ab sin C / 2. nr-p15-teaching-prose supplies the supplementary-sine identity. For 0 < C < 180 degrees, sine is at most one and equals one at 90 degrees.
findings.assumptions: The elementary sine bound is available from prior right-angled trigonometry; a calculator can support exploration.

repair.proposal: Optional task after nr-p37-proof: Two sides of a triangle are 6 cm and 10 cm, with included angle 0 < C < 180 degrees. Find the greatest possible area and the angle where it occurs. Explain why C = 40 degrees and C = 140 degrees give equal areas. Generalise for fixed positive side lengths a and b. Expected answer: A = 30 sin C cm², with maximum 30 cm² at 90 degrees. Supplementary angles have equal sines and therefore equal areas. In general the maximum is ab/2 at 90 degrees.

findings.doneWhen: Students justify the maximum and supplementary-angle equality using the area formula.

findings.finding: The written givens do not select between two possible included angles.
findings.breakdown: The area equation gives sin C = 9.23/27. Both approximately 20 degrees and 160 degrees satisfy the area and adjacent side lengths. Automatically choosing the calculator’s acute result overlooks the supplementary solution explicitly taught earlier.
findings.checked: nr-p32-rule supplies the area equation, nr-p12-equations rehearses inverse sine, and nr-p15-teaching-prose explains supplementary solutions. Neither the stem nor the mathematical givens in nr-p42-q9d specifies an acute angle. The diagram is explicitly not to scale, and nr-p42-q9c is a separate task with different givens.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator is available. The acute-looking, not-to-scale outline does not reliably select the intended solution.

repair.proposal: Add to nr-p42-q9d: 'Angle ACB is acute.'

findings.doneWhen: The givens select exactly one angle satisfying the area equation.

findings.finding: Explain why two sides and one angle do not always permit an immediate sine-rule calculation.
findings.breakdown: Returns to the opposite-pair criterion and asks students to explain method selection using contrasting configurations.
findings.checked: In 10c, the known 15 cm side is opposite 85 degrees and the requested angle is opposite 12 cm. In 10d, 85 degrees is included between 12 cm and 15 cm, so its opposite side must first be found. nr-p13-teaching-criteria and nr-p19-requirements teach both decisions.
findings.assumptions: Only methods already taught by the end of topic 7 are required.

repair.proposal: Optional task after nr-p42-q10d: Compare 10c and 10d. Both give two sides and one angle. Explain why the sine rule can be used immediately in 10c but needs preparation in 10d. State a general test for using it immediately. Expected answer: 10c supplies the complete opposite pair 15 cm and 85 degrees. In 10d, first find the side opposite 85 degrees using the cosine rule. An immediate sine-rule calculation needs a known side and its known opposite angle, plus the known opposite partner of the requested unknown.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the opposite-pair test and the necessary preliminary calculation in 10d.
